title: Can Caring Make Us Careless
author: Murray Sutcliffe
summary: Murray Sutcliffe argues that good intentions in teaching are comforting but are not evidence that students are learning. Opening with a student-teaching memory from Pretoria, he shows how two equally caring teachers can make opposite decisions about what students need, one prioritising freedom and safety, the other rigour and high standards. Drawing on Jonathan Haidt's elephant and rider metaphor, he suggests teachers often start from moral intuition about what good teaching looks like and then defend the methods that match it. He confesses to vibe teaching, making English lessons fun without any evidence it helped, and warns that the appearance of freedom or compliance in a classroom is not proof of what is learned. He concedes that evidence cannot settle what education is for, invoking Dylan Wiliam's opportunity cost, and closes by admitting that in sparing students hardship he risked expecting less of them.
points: Caring about students does not tell teachers what that care should look like, so intentions need to be paired with the questions of what is being achieved, why it is believed right, and what is actually happening as a result.
Teachers, like moral reasoners in Haidt's model, tend to let intuition choose the method and reasoning merely justify it, which makes it hard to weigh evidence that challenges favoured practices.
What a classroom looks like is not the same as what students are learning; the appearance of freedom does not prove independence, and the appearance of compliance does not rule it out.
Evidence about what works cannot say what education is for, and every worthwhile aim carries an opportunity cost, so purposes must be argued openly rather than assumed.
Over-sensitivity to students' hardships can quietly lower expectations, which is the real danger of good intentions.
quotes: Good intentions are important. They establish what we’re trying to achieve and why it matters. However, they cannot, by themselves, demonstrate that we’ve achieved it.
Because caring about our students doesn’t mean we agree on what that care should look like.
We develop an idea of what good teaching should look like, informed by our values and experiences, and then find ourselves defending the methods that most closely resemble that ideal.
The appearance of freedom is not proof of intellectual independence, just as the appearance of compliance is not proof of its absence.
It doesn’t make for a particularly inspiring pitch, but sometimes learning does just need to be endured.
Evidence can inform our practice and help us make better decisions about students learning, but it can’t tell us what learning is for.
In trying to be sensitive to their circumstances, I risked expecting less of them. And that is the greatest danger of good intentions.
